content: Microcytic anemia is defined by the presence of red blood cells that are smaller than normal. The normal range for mean corpuscular volume (MCV), which is a measure of the average size of red blood cells, is between 76 and 100 femtoliters (fL). Red blood cells with an MCV below 76 fL are classified as microcytic, while those with an MCV above 100 fL are considered macrocytic. In microcytic anemia, the red blood cells (erythrocytes) are often hypochromic, meaning they appear paler than normal due to reduced hemoglobin content. This can be quantified using the mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), which measures the amount of hemoglobin per red blood cell. The normal MCH range is 27–32 picograms (pg). Another related parameter is the mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC), which reflects the concentration of hemoglobin in a given volume of red blood cells. The normal MCHC range is approximately 320–360 g/L or 32–36 g/dL. Consequently, microcytic anemia is typically described as microcytic, hypochromic anemia. The most common cause of microcytic anemia is iron deficiency anemia, which is also the leading cause of anemia overall. Other causes include thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia (which can be congenital or acquired), and, less commonly, anemia of chronic disease (although this more frequently results in normochromic, normocytic anemia). Rarely, lead poisoning can also lead to microcytic anemia. It is important to note that conditions typically associated with normocytic or macrocytic anemia should also be considered, as the coexistence of multiple causes of anemia can obscure the classic presentation of each type. To differentiate microcytic anemia from other diseases, a thorough review of the differential diagnosis of anemia is essential.
